# Introduction

In this unit, I learned about moderator and mediator variables by reading Baron and Kenny (1986). Both concepts involve a third variable, but they have different purposes. A moderator explains when or for whom an effect changes. A mediator explains how or why an effect happens. The article also explains that they require different statistical tests.

# Moderator Variables

A moderator changes the direction or strength of the relationship between an independent variable and a dependent variable. For example, an online advertisement may increase purchase intention for one consumer group but not for another group. In this case, the consumer group may be a moderator. Moderation is usually tested with an interaction term. The model includes the independent variable, moderator, and their interaction. A significant interaction means that the effect of the independent variable changes depending on the moderator. ANOVA can be used when the variables are categorical. Regression with an interaction term can be used when the variables are continuous.

# Mediator Variables

A mediator explains the process through which an independent variable affects a dependent variable. For example, an advertisement may create a positive emotion, and the emotion may then increase purchase intention. In this case, emotion may be a mediator.

Baron and Kenny recommend three regression steps:
1. Test whether the independent variable affects the mediator.
2. Test whether the independent variable affects the dependent variable.
3. Test whether the mediator affects the dependent variable after controlling for the independent variable.

The effect of the independent variable should become smaller after the mediator is added. Complete mediation occurs when the direct effect disappears. Partial mediation occurs when the effect becomes smaller but remains.

# Difference Between Moderation and Mediation

The easiest way for me to remember the difference is:
- A moderator explains when or for whom an effect changes.
- A mediator explains how or why an effect happens.

Moderation is tested with an interaction effect. Mediation is tested by examining the relationships among the independent variable, mediator, and dependent variable. The choice should be based on the research question and theory, not only on the statistical results.

# Important Issues

Measurement error may make a mediator appear weaker than it actually is. It may also make the direct effect of the independent variable appear stronger. Regression analysis also does not prove causality. Researchers need theory and an appropriate research design to explain why the independent variable causes the mediator and why the mediator affects the dependent variable. The article also explains that moderation and mediation can be included in the same model. A moderator can show which consumers respond differently, while a mediator can explain why they respond differently.

# Main Points I Learned
- Moderator and mediator are different concepts.
- A moderator changes the strength or direction of a relationship.
- A mediator explains the process behind a relationship.
- Moderation requires an interaction term.
- Mediation requires testing several relationships.
- Measurement error can affect mediation results.
- Statistical results alone cannot prove causality.
- Theory should guide the selection of the model.

# Conclusion

This article helped me understand the basic difference between moderator and mediator variables. A moderator shows when an effect changes, while a mediator explains how the effect happens. This distinction is important because each concept needs a different statistical analysis. I should first consider the theoretical role of a variable before selecting the analysis.

# References

Baron, Reuben M., and David A. Kenny. 1986. “The Moderator–Mediator Variable Distinction in Social Psychological Research: Conceptual, Strategic, and Statistical Considerations.” *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology* 51 (6): 1173–1182. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.51.6.1173.
